beats.intro: Chapter one. [[sub]]A company keeps two sets of books: one for investors, and one for the tax authority. This chapter shows why the two profits differ, and what that means for an analyst.
beats.ledgers: Take one business and two different rulebooks. [[acc]]Accounting standards give accounting profit, also called pre-tax income. The tax charged on it in the income statement is income tax expense. [[tax]]Tax law gives taxable income. The tax on that is income tax payable, the amount actually owed. [[gap]]When the two profits differ, expense and payable differ too. The balance sheet records the gap as a deferred tax asset or liability.
beats.gap: Here is where a gap comes from. Equipment costs twenty thousand pounds. [[book]]For accounting, depreciate it over ten years. Its carrying amount falls slowly. [[taxl]]Tax law allows seven years, so the tax base falls faster. [[open]]The shaded space between the lines is a temporary difference. It opens in the early years, and peaks at year seven. [[close]]Then it closes, and is gone by year ten, when both lines reach zero. [[perm]]A permanent difference never closes. Dividends from a subsidiary, for example, are never taxed. Profit and taxable income differ for good, and no deferred tax appears.
beats.reston: Now the numbers, with tax at thirty percent. [[y1]]In year one, accounting profit is four thousand seven hundred. Taxable income is lower, three thousand eight hundred forty three, because tax depreciation is bigger. [[pay]]Tax payable is thirty percent of taxable income: eleven fifty three. [[def]]The deferred tax liability grows by two fifty seven. [[exp]]Add them. Income tax expense is fourteen ten, exactly thirty percent of accounting profit. [[all]]Years two and three work the same way. Payable follows taxable income, and the liability adds two fifty seven each year, reaching seven seventy one by year three.
beats.rules: Here is the rule for any item on the balance sheet. Compare its carrying amount, the book value, with its tax base. [[asset]]For an asset, a carrying amount above the tax base gives a deferred tax liability. Below the tax base, a deferred tax asset. [[liab]]For a liability, it flips. A carrying amount above the tax base gives a deferred tax asset, and below gives a liability. [[why]]The logic is simple. A deferred tax liability means more tax to pay later. A deferred tax asset means tax was paid early, so less is owed later. [[ex]]Check Reston's equipment: carrying amount above tax base, so a liability. It matches.
beats.change: Deferred tax balances are recalculated at every balance sheet date, so they move when tax rates change. [[cut]]Say a temporary difference is one thousand, and the rate falls from thirty five percent to twenty one. A liability of three fifty shrinks to two ten. An asset shrinks the same way, because the future benefit is smaller. [[va]]A deferred tax asset is only worth recording if the company will have profits to use it. If that is doubtful, IFRS reverses the asset. US GAAP sets up a valuation allowance, which cuts the asset to the amount more likely than not to be realized. [[judg]]That takes management judgment, so analysts watch changes in the allowance. They move reported tax expense, and earnings.
beats.analyst: How should an analyst treat a deferred tax liability? [[debt]]If it is expected to reverse, and cash tax will be paid, treat it as a liability. [[eq]]If it will never reverse, because of continuing losses or a change in tax law, no cash goes out. Treat it as equity. [[none]]If both the amount and the timing of payment are uncertain, leave it out of both debt and equity.
beats.rates: Analysts use three tax rates. [[stat]]The statutory rate is the legal rate in the company's home country. [[eff]]The effective rate is income tax expense divided by pre-tax income. [[cash]]The cash tax rate is tax actually paid, divided by pre-tax income. [[ex]]For Reston in year one, the statutory rate is thirty percent. The effective rate is fourteen ten over forty seven hundred, also thirty percent. The cash rate is eleven fifty three over forty seven hundred, only twenty four point five percent. [[use]]Use the effective rate to forecast earnings, and the cash rate to forecast cash flow. The difference between them is the change in deferred tax.
beats.blend: An effective rate blends the rates of every country where profit is earned. [[setup]]Company ABC earns one hundred in Country A, taxed at forty percent, and one hundred in Country B, taxed at ten percent. Tax is fifty on two hundred: twenty five percent. [[grow]]Now Country B's profit grows fifteen percent a year, while A stays flat. More of the profit sits in the low tax country, so the blended rate slides, to about twenty four, twenty three, and twenty two percent by year three. [[note]]It is a weighted average, so the mix of profit matters.
beats.recon: Companies disclose a reconciliation from the statutory rate to the effective rate. [[start]]It starts at the statutory rate. [[items]]Then it adds or subtracts items: lower foreign tax rates, tax credits such as research credits, expenses that are not deductible, and adjustments to prior years. [[end]]What is left is the effective rate. [[read]]The analyst's question is which items will repeat and which are one-time, because that decides what rate to forecast. These figures are illustrative.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]Accounting profit drives income tax expense. Taxable income drives income tax payable. [[w2]]Temporary differences reverse and create deferred tax. Permanent differences do not. [[w3]]Tax expense equals tax payable plus the change in deferred tax. [[w4]]Compare the statutory, effective and cash tax rates, and read the rate reconciliation.
